t: Maximum Manhattan Distance After All Moves — Axis Counting
o: Each fixed letter commits ±1 on one axis; each '_' is free and can be anything. Manhattan distance is |x| + |y|, and each '_' can add 1 to whichever axis we boost. On the horizontal axis the net displacement is R − L, and all c underscores can push it further in the sign of that net value, giving |R − L| + c; symmetrically vertical gives |U − D| + c. The answer is the max of the two. Example 1: dx = −1, dy = −1, c = 2 → max(1+2, 1+2) = 4. Example 2: dx = 1, dy = 1, c = 1 → max(2, 2) = 3.
k: Manhattan distance separates by axis, and every '_' independently contributes +1 to whichever axis it is assigned, so never split underscores between axes.
The optimum is simply max(|R−L| + c, |U−D| + c) where c is the underscore count.
This is a pure counting problem — no simulation or search is needed.

a.i: Count the four letters and the underscores. Assigning all underscores along the dominant direction of one axis maximizes that axis's absolute displacement; taking the better of the two axes is optimal because each underscore is worth exactly +1 wherever it goes.
s: Compute dx = R − L and dy = U − D.

a.i: Instead of counting, propagate the interval of reachable x-coordinates [xmin, xmax] and y-coordinates [ymin, ymax]. A fixed letter shifts both endpoints; an underscore widens each interval by 1 on both sides (it can go either way). The farthest Manhattan point is the combination of the extreme of each interval.
s: Start with x-interval and y-interval both [0, 0].
For each character, shift both endpoints (fixed letter) or expand each interval by 1 in both directions ('_').
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the string

w: Prefer the counting formula in an interview — it is shorter and easier to justify; the interval view generalizes nicely (e.g., if '_' could be replaced by any of several directions, or if you needed Chebyshev distance instead). Pitfalls: trying to split underscores across axes (never helps since each is worth +1 anywhere), and miscomputing signs for L/D. Follow-ups: maximize distance at an intermediate time step, or minimize the maximum distance instead.
